title: Slit-Scan
description: Ten seconds of a two-car train running past an old wooden country station in low evening sun, shown so that every point of the picture is at its own moment. Left is now, right is a few seconds ago, and in between time climbs on average exactly as fast as the train runs, along a front that rests already bent: across the windows it climbs faster than the train, so the train folds back on itself and its windows come out as mirrored X shapes, then slower, so doors and pillars are drawn out. Each row is also set at its own moment by where that rope lies, up to two seconds apart, so the front cuts through the end of the train: some rows already show the empty station where it has gone, others still carry carriage, and the train comes out as a carved, curved silhouette with the platform showing through it. Nothing is blended between moments: the picture is laid in hard strata, each one frame of the clip, and where two moments meet the seam frays into fine single-line striations. The bends drift slowly. Press and drag and the front follows your hand like a rope, and the edge between train and empty station goes with it; hold and it steepens. The station, the fence and the parked cars never moved, so they stay perfectly sharp whatever you do. Let go and it eases back.
intent: Time displacement after Zbigniew Rybczyński's time-slicing work and Adam Magyar's Stainless (2010-11, https://nautil.us/a-photographer-who-tinkers-with-time-234772), and herb's generative reference 2 (a street photo whose region is pulled into rigid strips). One process pushed to the edge: a real slit-scan over real footage. The stabilised clip's moving band is decoded with WebCodecs into a ring of 157 frames (luma full-res, chroma half) and every output pixel samples t = clock - D(x, y), with D a single sculpted time front whose ramp is as wide as the train runs in `depth` seconds, so its mean slope is exactly 1/v; D is spent along the train's measured run. The rope that marks the front's half-way point rests bent at two rows through the windows and breathes, so the local slope crosses 1/v several times and the first frame already shows the mirrored windows and drawn-out doors only a slit-scan can make; the pointer drags the rope further, read through a cubic B-spline so the train's magnification has no kinks. The rope also sets each row's moment: every row is offset by 6 s per print width that its rope stands right of the line's centre, so the bent rows and the rows beside them sit a few hundred ms to about 2 s apart, and the time front cuts through the train's tail along a curve that follows the rope. Every row also sits 0.5 s later, so the clock rests at 8.8 s with the front already in the tail: the roof and window rows are cut back to the empty station either side and hold carriage only where the front folds it, the rows below still carry the whole car. The clock runs six times faster through the stretch where the rest pose is only the empty station (one still plate, so nothing visible is skipped). Time is discrete, as a slit-scan's is: every pixel is locked to the nearest whole ring frame, never blended or followed along the motion, and D is read once per 2-device-px slit cell, so the train is laid in hard strata bounded by the front's isochrones (at 15 fps a frame is ~44 px of the train's run, so along a ribbon the strata are rigid slices of carriage). The rounding threshold steps through eight van der Corput phases, 0.4 frame wide, down every eight slit rows, so each seam between two moments frays into single-slit striations. Pixels on the occluder mask (fence and grass in front of the train) and static pixels are drawn from a median plate of the empty station, so nothing that stood still ever moves. ?t=seconds holds the clock (the hero is ?t=8.8), ?front=flat shows the clip as shot, ?slit=x,lean, ?depth=seconds (also the ramp's width), ?bend=y,x;... sets the rest bends (none for the plain ramp). Where the isochrones run across the rows (where the front cuts the train's end) whole frames would step the end ~44 px at a time, so there each stratum's frame is shifted by the train's measured run over the sub-frame remainder (never blended), with the tracked nose and tail deciding train from station: the cut is a smooth curve that frays only in the single-slit striations. Below the red stripe each slit column is held at the moment of the stripe directly above it, so the undercarriage never streaks and continues the body's cut as fine vertical slivers.

sources.note: 1920x1080 29.97 fps; Ohmi Railway, Koka, Shiga. Seconds 14-32 used: stabilised (phase correlation on the station roof, Lanczos warp), median plate from 14-21 s, band rows 256-704 of 21.5-32 s at 15 fps as VP9 (and H.264 fallback), occluder mask and train track (tools/depth/bakes/slit-scan/).
